catalog_quote: 1.4. Scope and limitation of this study ... This study is also limited to morphosyntactic phenomena; no attempt is made to describe the phonology in detail although a brief sketch is given in sections 1.5. and 1.6. 1.5. Segmental phonology In this section a brief statement of the segmental phonology is given as background information. The description follows basically Ohlson (no date a). Eastern Bontoc has two syllable types: CV and CVC. Examples are pa.yak 'feather', no.wang 'carabao', pa.pa 'duck', and qaw.ni 'later'. Stress is unpredictable, although it usually occurs on the penultimate syllable. There are few contrastive sets: 'kayyang 'blackbird' and kay'yang 'to throw a spear'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically determined (not predictable from phonological shape), but the default/usual position is the penultimate syllable; a small number of minimal pairs contrast antepenult-vs-final or penult-vs-final placement, e.g. 'kayyang 'blackbird' vs kay'yang 'to throw a spear' (stress mark written before the stressed syllable). Stress is therefore phonemic but with a strong penultimate tendency.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the remark that contrastive sets are 'few', with the one minimal pair kayyang cited; no conditioning by syllable weight, closed syllables, or affixation is stated in the stress sentence (sec. 1.6 Morphophonemics on pp. 16-17 describes vowel deletion under affixation without mentioning stress shift).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (stress positions in disyllabic citation forms; the pair is given as bare roots). The author states explicitly that the study 'is also limited to morphosyntactic phenomena; no attempt is made to describe the phonology in detail' (p. 14) and that the sketch follows an unpublished SIL manuscript, Ohlson n.d.(a) 'Phonology of Southern Bontoc' (Barlig dialect); the stress statement is nonetheless in Fukuda's own voice from 1977-80 fieldwork in Kadaclan.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Kadaclan (Kadaklan, 'Kenachakran') dialect of Eastern Bontoc (Fukuda 1997 sec. 1.2, p. 11: 'Language data used in this study are from the Kadaclan dialect of Eastern Bontoc'), i.e. the ISO ebk half of fina1242; Fukuda's phonology sketch 'follows basically Ohlson (no date a)', an unpublished SIL ms on the Barlig dialect (Ohlson calls the language 'Southern Bontoc', which Fukuda fn. 4 p. 13 equates with his 'Eastern'). Reid's ISO change request 2009-073 (Reid, submitter) separates Talubin/Bayyo as Southern Bontok [obk]; Glottolog 5.1 keeps both under fina1242, so the quote covers only the Eastern (Kadaklan/Barlig/Lias) side. No Glottolog dialect-level code for Kadaklan was seen. Distinct from Central Bontok cent2292 (Reid 1963, already in the catalog).

sources.citation: Boersma, Paul and Benz, Anton and Mattausch, Jason (2011). A programme for bidirectional phonology and phonetics and their acquisition and evolution. In Bidirectional Optimality Theory. John Benjamins. pp. 33-72.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online (also online with a university library login)
sources.note: A general theory paper on the bidirectional phonology-phonetics (BiPhon) model. The words Bontoc/Bontok/Finallig/Kadaclan/Philippines do not occur anywhere in the text; stress is discussed only abstractly (hypothetical iambic and trochaic languages, Greek, Latin). The Glottolog attachment of this work to fina1242 is a misattribution. Author is Boersma alone; Benz and Mattausch are the volume editors.

sources.note: The paper is about discourse markers and particles in Ga'dang, Ilocano, Central Bontoc, Ifugao and Finallig (Barlig). It gives a 23-item list of Finallig (Barlig) particles (PDF pp. 8-9) with glosses but no stress marks and no statement about word stress; the only 'prosody' remarks concern the intonational/laryngeal prosody of Ga'dang interjections and a general note on phonological prosody. Nothing on where stress falls in any Bontoc variety.
